articles.title: Check before you share

body.support:
Every post is made by someone, for a reason. Some posts want to make you angry or scared. Why? Because angry and scared people **share**.

Sort what you read:

1. A **fact** can be checked: “The game starts at 7pm.”
2. An **opinion** is what someone thinks: “It's the best game ever.”
3. A **feeling** is how someone feels: “I'm so excited!”

Fake posts use big words like *shocking* or *banned*. They want you to react fast.

AI can make fake photos too.

Before you share, use **SIFT**:

**Stop.** **Investigate** who posted it. **Find** what others say. **Trace** where it came from.
body.core:
Every post is made by someone, for a reason. Some want to inform you. Some want to sell to you. Some want to make you angry, scared or excited — because angry, scared and excited people **share**.

Start by sorting what you're reading:

1. A **fact** can be checked: “The game starts at 7pm.”
2. An **opinion** is what someone thinks: “It'll be the best game of the year.”
3. A **feeling** is how someone feels: “I'm so excited!”

Fake posts mix these up. They use **loaded** words — *shocking*, *banned*, *they don't want you to know* — to make an opinion feel like a fact. Fair, **objective** writing sticks to facts. **Subjective** writing is full of feelings and opinions.

Photos and videos can be faked too. AI tools can now make a realistic picture of anyone, doing anything.

So before you share, use **SIFT**: **Stop**. **Investigate** the source. **Find** better coverage. **Trace** it back to where it started.
body.extend:
Every post is made by someone, for a reason. Some want to inform you. Some want to sell to you. Some want to make you angry, scared or excited — because emotional people **share**.

Start by sorting what you're reading:

1. A **fact** can be checked: “The game starts at 7pm.”
2. An **opinion** is what someone thinks: “It'll be the best game of the year.”
3. A **feeling** is how someone feels: “I'm so excited!”

Fake or slanted posts blur these. They use **loaded** language — *shocking*, *banned*, *they don't want you to know* — to dress an opinion up as a fact. **Objective** writing sticks to evidence; **subjective** writing is coloured by feelings and opinions. Even real news can show **bias** through what it includes, leaves out, or which quotes it picks.

Context matters too. A post reflects when and why it was made: the puffer-jacket Pope spread in 2023, the year AI image tools went mainstream and most people didn't yet know what they could do.

Before you share, use **SIFT**: **Stop**. **Investigate** the source. **Find** better coverage. **Trace** claims, quotes and images back to where they started.

caseStudies.title: The puffer-jacket Pope

body.support:
In March 2023, a photo of **Pope Francis** in a big white puffer jacket went viral. Many people thought it was real.

It was fake. It was made with an **AI tool called Midjourney**.

There were clues, like blurry hands. But most people didn't look closely. They just shared it.
body.core:
In March 2023, an image of **Pope Francis** wearing a long white puffer jacket appeared online. It looked like a real photo. It was shared all over Twitter and TikTok, and many people believed it.

It wasn't real. Fact-checkers found it had been made with an **AI image tool called Midjourney** and first posted on Reddit.

NBC News called it one of the first times AI-made misinformation spread on a huge scale. Clues were there — blurry hands, odd details — but most people didn't look closely before sharing.

caseStudies.title: Australia's fact-checkers

body.support:
**AAP FactCheck** is an Australian team. It checks posts and claims that are spreading online.

It finds where a claim came from. It asks experts. It checks other trusted sources. Then it says if the claim is true or not.

You can do the same steps yourself.
body.core:
**AAP FactCheck** is a team at Australian Associated Press. AAP is a national news agency. The team checks claims that spread online. It checks social media posts, viral videos and what public figures say.

First it looks for where a claim came from. Then it asks experts. It also checks what other trusted sources say. Then it shares what it found, with a verdict such as **False** or **Misleading**.

You can do the same steps yourself. It only takes a few minutes.

teacher.overview: Students learn to separate fact, opinion and feeling, recognise loaded and subjective language, and check claims using **SIFT** (Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims to the original — a method developed by Mike Caulfield). The real cases are the AI-generated ‘puffer-jacket Pope’ image (2023) and how AAP FactCheck works.
prep: Find one current, harmless viral claim to model SIFT live (check it yourself first).
Have AAP FactCheck open to show a real fact-check.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Fact, opinion, feeling
steps: **Hook (5 min):** show the Pope image — real or fake? Vote, then reveal.
**Explicit teaching (15 min):** fact / opinion / feeling; model with sentences about a local event.
**Read (15 min):** Check before you share + questions.
**Exit:** one of each about today's lunch.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Spot the spin
steps: **Model (10 min):** annotate the dodgy post together.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — SIFT it
steps: **Case study (15 min):** the puffer-jacket Pope; context and technology.
**Model SIFT live (15 min):** check a current claim, thinking aloud.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Fact-check it
steps: **Write (30 min):** final mission. Fast finishers: Level Up (compare two reports).
**Check & reflect (15 min):** quick check, reflection, request sign-off.

teacher.answers:
**Fact, opinion or feeling?** Opens Saturday 9am — Fact. Best skate park — Opinion. So pumped — Feeling. $1.2 million — Fact. Should have gone to the library — Opinion. Makes me furious — Feeling.

**Dodgy post:** 1 new, vague account; 2 alarm words; 3 big claim with no source; 4 pressure to share; 5 any photo can be reused; 6 shares don't prove truth.

**Take out the spin (sample):** “A local teenager helped rescue …”; “The team lost 0–5.”; “A new rule restricts phone use; some students disagree.”

**Case study:** made with Midjourney; first posted on Reddit (March 2023); spread on Twitter/TikTok.
